sections.h2: Do squatters have rights in Texas?
sections.html:
Texas has no law that rewards simply moving into someone else's property, but a long, open and hostile occupation can eventually turn into ownership through adverse possession. Separately, a newer removal process lets owners clear certain trespassers without a full lawsuit.

These are two different tracks. Adverse possession is about who holds title after years of occupation, and it is decided in a trespass to try title case. Removal of an intruder is about getting someone out of a property now. A homeowner preparing to sell needs to know which situation applies, because a person living in the house can complicate a closing.

If you are unsure which track fits, start by writing down when the occupant arrived, whether you ever gave permission, and what happened when you asked them to leave.

sections.h2: How does Texas define adverse possession?
sections.html:
The Civil Practice and Remedies Code defines it as an actual and visible appropriation of real property, begun and continued under a claim of right that is inconsistent with and hostile to the claim of another person (Section 16.021(1)).

Each word in that definition does work. The possession must be visible, so a neighbor or owner can see it. It must rest on a claim of right, and it must be hostile to the owner, meaning the possessor does not hold with the owner's permission. A tenant paying rent, for example, holds with permission and is not hostile to the landlord's title.

The Texas courts' published opinions describe the claim as one brought through a trespass to try title suit, in which a judge decides who holds the better title.

sections.h2: What time period does adverse possession need in Texas?
sections.html:
The best known period is ten years under Section 16.026, and title passes if the possessor stays for the whole period and meets the statutory requirements. Shorter periods exist where the possessor has paper title.

Adverse possession periods described in Texas court opinions
SectionPeriodKey condition
16.0243 yearsPeaceable adverse possession under title or color of title
16.0255 yearsPossessor cultivates, uses or enjoys the land, pays taxes and claims under a duly registered deed
16.02610 yearsContinuous possession meeting the statutory requirements

Sources: Texas Courts opinion on adverse possession and Fourteenth Court of Appeals opinion. The shorter periods come from an older appeals opinion, so confirm the current statute text with an attorney before relying on them.

sections.h2: How can a Texas owner remove squatters?
sections.html:
Chapter 24B of the Property Code lets an owner file a request for removal with the sheriff or constable, with no court case required, when certain conditions are met.

  • The occupant stayed after being told to leave.
  • The property was not open to the public when the occupant entered.
  • No lawsuit is pending between the owner and the occupant.
  • The occupant is not a family member or a current or former tenant.

An owner who uses the process wrongly can be sued under Section 24B.005, so accuracy on the request matters. When the person is a tenant or former tenant, the removal process does not fit, and the owner turns to the eviction route instead.

sections.h2: What does the eviction route look like?
sections.html:
Eviction starts with written notice to vacate, usually three days or more, or whatever longer period the lease sets, and then a suit in justice court. The State Law Library describes the steps in its eviction guide.

The tenant must be served at least four days before trial. The hearing is set no sooner than 10 days and no later than 21 days after filing. Either side may appeal to county court within five days of judgment. After a final judgment, a writ of possession becomes available six days later, and an officer must give 24 hours' notice before removal.

The guide also describes a summary disposition procedure, Section 24.0051606, for squatters in a forcible entry and detainer suit. The response is due in four days, and a disputed case goes to trial between 10 and 21 days after filing.

sections.h2: How does a squatter or adverse possessor affect selling a house?
sections.html:
An occupant with no lease can delay a sale because buyers and lenders want to receive the property vacant, and a title company may refuse to insure over an open ownership claim. Resolve the occupancy first, or tell the buyer exactly what is going on.

Keep the evidence that you own and control the property: the deed, recent tax bills and any written notices you served. Paid tax records help show who has been treated as the owner. If you are the person who has occupied a property for years, speak to a lawyer before you claim anything, because a mistake can cost the whole claim.

  • Do not change locks or cut utilities on a tenant without legal advice.
  • Photograph the property and keep dated copies of every notice.
  • Ask the sheriff or constable's office how to submit a removal request.

sections.h2: How do property taxes figure into an adverse possession claim?
sections.html:
Tax payment is part of the five-year rule in Section 16.025, which asks that the possessor pay taxes and hold under a duly registered deed. For owners, a clean tax record is useful evidence that you have acted as the owner.

The Comptroller says the owner at the start of the year decides who owes that year's tax, and in most cases a bill still unpaid on February 1 is delinquent. An owner who lets the bill lapse while someone else occupies the house invites a second problem on top of the first.

sections.h2: What does a wrongful removal look like and what are the risks?
sections.html:
Using the sheriff or constable process against a person who is really a tenant or family member exposes the owner to a lawsuit under Section 24B.005. That is why the four conditions in the statute matter.

Before filing, an owner should check whether the occupant ever paid rent or had permission to stay, whether any suit between the two of you is pending, and whether the property was open to the public when the person entered. If the answers are unclear, a justice court eviction case gives both sides a hearing and a written judgment, which is a safer base for a sale contract.

The justice court rules do not cover the notice you must send before suing. Those are in Chapter 24 of the Property Code, and the State Law Library notes that a 30-day federal notice may apply to covered properties. Check your property's status before you serve a three-day notice.

A seller who has been through any of this should tell the title company at the start, since a past dispute can show up in the records they search.

faqs.q: How many years of adverse possession does Texas require?
faqs.a: Ten years is the best known period under Section 16.026. Shorter periods of 3 and 5 years apply in narrower situations that involve title or a registered deed.

faqs.q: Can a tenant claim adverse possession of a rental?
faqs.a: A tenant who pays rent holds with the owner's permission, so the possession is not hostile to the owner. Hostility is part of the statutory definition.

faqs.q: Can I remove a squatter without going to court?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Chapter 24B allows a removal request to the sheriff or constable when the occupant is not a family member or current or former tenant and no suit is pending between you.

faqs.q: How long does a Texas eviction take?
faqs.a: Hearing dates fall 10 to 21 days after filing, and a writ of possession is available six days after final judgment. Appeals and other issues can add time.

faqs.q: Can squatters stop me from selling my house?
faqs.a: They can delay it, since buyers and title companies want a clear title and vacant possession. Sort out the occupancy with an attorney before you list.
